'''Anthony David <!-- NOTE: Do not add "Tony" here per [[WP:HYPOCORISM]]--> Gonzalez''' (born February 27, 1976) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] [[tight end]] who played in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) for 17 seasons. Gonzalez spent his first 12 seasons with the [[Kansas City Chiefs]], who selected him in the first round of the [[1997 NFL draft]]. During his last five seasons, he was a member of the [[Atlanta Falcons]]. Since retiring in 2013, Gonzalez has served as a football analyst for ''[[NFL on Prime Video]]'' and was previously at [[CBS Sports]] and [[Fox Sports]].

Regarded as one of the greatest tight ends of all time, Gonzalez is the NFL's all-time leader in receptions and receiving yards by a tight end, and he ranks second in receiving touchdowns. Gonzalez earned 14 [[Pro Bowl]] selections and six first-team [[All-Pro]] selections during his career, both of which are records for a tight end. Gonzalez was known for his durability, appearing in 270 of 272 regular season games and losing only two fumbles on 1,327 touches. He was inducted to the [[Pro Football Hall of Fame]] in 2019, his first year of eligibility.

'''Ante Josip "Tony" Mandarich''' (born September 23, 1966) is a Canadian former professional [[American football|football]] [[Tackle (gridiron football position)|tackle]] who played in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) for seven seasons. Referred to as "the best offensive line prospect ever" during his [[college football]] career with the [[Michigan State Spartans football|Michigan State Spartans]],<ref name="Most Popular">{{cite news | url=http://vault.sportsillustrated.cnn.com/vault/cover/featured/9169/index.htm | work=CNN | title=Most Popular | access-date=May 25, 2010 | archive-date=March 10, 2009 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090310160520/http://vault.sportsillustrated.cnn.com/vault/cover/featured/9169/index.htm | url-status=dead }}</ref> he won [[UPI Lineman of the Year (College)|UPI Lineman of the Year]] in 1988. Mandarich was selected second overall by the [[Green Bay Packers]] in the [[1989 NFL draft]], but was unable to meet expectations and released after four seasons. Following five years away from football, he returned with the [[Indianapolis Colts]], where he spent his last three seasons. He is the only top five pick in his draft class not inducted to the [[Pro Football Hall of Fame]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.pennlive.com/sports/2019/04/e60-on-how-tony-mandarich-survived-bust-amid-legendary-1989-nfl-draft-class-shed-steroids-and-painkillers-to-live-again.html|title=How Tony Mandarich survived legendary 1989 NFL Draft class bust, shed steroids and painkillers to live again|last=Jones|first=David|date=April 22, 2019|website=pennlive.com|language=en-US|access-date=April 24, 2019}}</ref><ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite AV media |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?si=oj-uWhNV-GlOpidk&v=PuxK2RhxpNg&feature=youtu.be |title=Top 10 Draft Busts |date=2020-04-10 |last=Isaac Green |access-date=2025-03-30 |via=YouTube}} Originally broadcast by [[NFL Network]] in 2007.</ref>

'''Tony Dale Galbreath'''  (born January 29, 1954) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[running back]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) for the [[New Orleans Saints]], [[Minnesota Vikings]], and [[New York Giants]].<ref>{{cite news |last=Sigler |first=John |date=August 15, 2019 |title=The top 100 players in New Orleans Saints history |url=https://www.shreveporttimes.com/story/sports/nfl/saints/2019/08/15/sigler-top-100-players-new-orleans-saints-history/2019459001/ |work=[[The Times (Shreveport)|The Times]] |access-date=March 6, 2021}}</ref> He played [[college football]] for the [[Missouri Tigers football|Missouri Tigers]] and was selected in the second round of the [[1976 NFL draft]].

Galbreath was an All-Big Eight running back for the Missouri Tigers in 1974. He was elected team captain for the 1975 season and still ranks among the Tigers' all-time leading rushers, despite the fact that he played just two years of football after transferring from Indian Hill ([[Iowa]]) Junior College.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Tony Galbreath – Missouri Sports Hall of Fame |url=https://mosportshalloffame.com/inductees/tony-galbreath/ |access-date=2023-06-13 |language=en-US}}</ref>

Galbreath was a rookie in 1976 with the New Orleans Saints and was part of the "Thunder and Lightning" backfield, along with Saints' first round pick [[Chuck Muncie]]. Galbreath quickly became one of the top pass-catching running backs in the NFL. As a rookie, he was the NFL's sixth leading receiver. In 1978, his third season with the Saints, he finished second in the NFL in receiving. He played with the Saints for five seasons, and when he left the Saints, he ranked second in all-time rushing yards for the team.

Galbreath was traded to the Minnesota Vikings in 1981. He played three years for the Vikings, primarily as a pass-catching back and blocker. Galbreath went to the New York Giants in 1984, essentially fulfilling the same role. He played four seasons with the Giants, including the 1986 season in which the Giants won the Super Bowl ([[Super Bowl XXI]]), as Galbreath was the team's second leading receiver. He retired after the 1987 season as the most prolific pass-catching running back in NFL history.

Galbreath was enshrined in the University of Missouri Athletics Hall of Fame in 1995. Galbreath was enshrined in the New Orleans Saints Hall of Fame in 1991. In 2013, he was enshrined in the Missouri Sports Hall of Fame. Galbreath's family resides in Fulton.

Hunter was selected by the [[Buffalo Bills]] in the first-round (12th overall) of the [[1983 NFL draft]], two picks ahead of Jim Kelly.<ref name="PFR2">{{Cite web |title=1983 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1983/draft.htm |access-date=June 2, 2024 |website=Pro Football Reference}}</ref> He split his four-year NFL career between the Bills and the [[Los Angeles Rams]], accumulating 134 receptions for 1501 yards with 9 touchdowns.<ref name="PFA">{{Cite web |url=https://www.profootballarchives.com/playerh/hunt06400.html |title=Tony Hunter Stats |website=Pro Football Archives |access-date=June 2, 2024 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230502202817/https://www.profootballarchives.com/playerh/hunt06400.html |archive-date=May 2, 2023}}</ref> His final season in 1986 was cut short due to a career ending leg injury.<ref name="BN 1987.09.02">{{cite news |title=Rams Say Goodbye to Hunter |newspaper=The Buffalo News (NY) |date=September 2, 1987 |page=C-5 |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-buffalo-news-rams-say-goodbye-to-to/148561934/
|via=Newspapers.com}}{{open access}}</ref>

Hunter died on June 11, 2024, at the age of 64.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.totalprosports.com/nfl/former-buffalo-bills-first-round-running-back-has-tragically-passes-away/ |title=Former Buffalo Bills First-Round Running Back Has Tragically Passes Away |first1=Alex |last1=Hoegler |website=Total Pro Sports |date=June 20, 2024 |access-date=June 22, 2024}}</ref>

'''Anthony Bernard Jones''' (born December 30, 1965) is an American former professional [[Gridiron football|football]] player who was a [[wide receiver]] for five seasons in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) with the [[Houston Oilers]], [[Atlanta Falcons]] and [[Arizona Cardinals]]; one season in the [[Canadian Football League]] with the [[Sacramento Gold Miners]] and two season in the [[World League of American Football]] with the [[Frankfurt Galaxy (NFL Europe)|Frankfurt Galaxy]] and the [[Amsterdam Admirals]]. He played [[college football]] for the [[Texas Longhorns football|Texas Longhorns]], earning all-conference honors in the [[Southwest Conference]] and the 1988 Astro-Bluebonnet Bowl Offensive MVP.

Jones attended [[Grapeland High School]], where he was a member of the 2A state champion basketball team in 1985.<ref>[https://www.uiltexas.org/files/leaguer/leaguer-archives/LE-1985-11.pdf 'The Leaguer, November 1985']. ''University Interscholastic League''. p. 13.</ref> 

He went on to attend the [[University of Texas at Austin]], where played football and ran track. In Football he was a 3x letterman, a 2x All-Conference Wide Receiver and a team captain. He set several school records including career receiving yards, most receiving yards in a game by a sophomore (still current), most receiving yards in a game, and most receiving yards and TD receptions in a bowl game.<ref>{{cite web |title=Texas Football Record Book |url=https://texaslonghorns.com/documents/2024/8/8/Football_Record_Book.pdf |access-date=6 November 2024}}</ref> In track, he was an All-American.<ref>[https://www.grapelandisd.net/Page/195 'The Next Level / Tony Jones - 1981-1985']. ''Grapeland Independent School District''.</ref> At the 1987 [[Southwest Conference]] championships, Jones ran the [[200 m]] in 20.28 seconds, a record that stood at the University of Texas for 32 years until it was broken in 2019 by Micaiah Harris, who ran a 20.21.<ref>[https://texassports.com/news/2019/5/26/track-field-cross-country-texas-track-field-concludes-west-prelims-with-20-entries-qualified-for-ncaa-championship.aspx 'Track & Field concludes West Prelims with 20 entries qualified for NCAA Championship']. ''University of Texas Athletics''. May 25, 2019.</ref> 

After college he played in the 1990 East-West Shrine game.<ref name="Honors">{{cite web |title=Texas Football Honors |url=https://texaslonghorns.com/documents/2024/8/8/Football_History___Honors.pdf |access-date=6 November 2024}}</ref>

Drafted by the Houston Oilers in the sixth round of the [[1990 NFL draft]], Jones was one of the smallest players in the league, weighing as little as 139 lb (63 kg) during his professional career.<ref>[https://oklahoman.com/article/2381494/in-the-nfl-bulk-is-in-293-players-on-veteran-rosters-weigh-275-or-more 'In the NFL, Bulk Is In 293 Players on Veteran Rosters Weigh 275 or More']. He was then signed by the Atlanta Falcons before the 1992 season, but only played in 10 games due to multiple injuries. He returned to the Oilers in 1993 and was cut at the end of camp, but then re-signed in the middle of the season and played 2 more games for them. He again became a free agent and was again signed by the Falcons in 1994, but cut by them before the camp started.<ref name="NFL">{{cite web |title=Tony Jones NFL Transactions |url=https://www.profootballarchives.com/players/j/jone22800.html |access-date=6 November 2024}}</ref>

After being release by the Falcons in 1994, Jones signed with the Sacramento Gold Miners of the CFL and played both receiver and returner. 

In 1995, he moved to the WLAF where he played for the Frankfurt Galaxy and helped them to [[World Bowl '95]], which they lost. In March of 1996 he was placed on the injured reserve by Frankfurt and in June 1996 he was signed by the Amsterdam Admirals as a late season replacement,<ref>{{cite news |title=Transactions |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=219AAAAAIBAJ&pg=PA14&dq=%22Tony+Jones%22+Frankfurt&article_id=3146,1372853&hl=en&sa=X&ved=2ahUKEwjU5KP0yN-OAxXdJ0QIHW22H1kQ6AF6BAgFEAM#v=onepage&q=%22Tony%20Jones%22%20Frankfurt&f=false |access-date=28 July 2025 |work=Times-Union |date=7 June 1996}}</ref> but only caught three passes.<ref>{{cite web |title=Tony Jones |url=https://profootballarchives.com/players/j/jone22800.html |access-date=6 November 2024}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=Transactions |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=NRImAAAAIBAJ&pg=PA8&dq=%22Tony+Jones%22+Frankfurt&article_id=4016,2319088&hl=en&sa=X&ved=2ahUKEwjU5KP0yN-OAxXdJ0QIHW22H1kQ6AF6BAgKEAM#v=onepage&q=%22Tony%20Jones%22%20Frankfurt&f=false |access-date=28 July 2025 |work=Gettysburg Times |date=23 March 1996}}</ref> During the 1996 WLAF season he was signed by the Arizona Cardinals who then released him during camp.<ref name="NFL"/>
